query: What are the requirements for approving an aircraft or component for return to service under 14 CFR Part 43?
answer:
Direct answer:
The supplied excerpts do not establish the specific requirements for approving an aircraft or component for return to service under 14 CFR Part 43; they only show that § 43.11 governs record entries for persons approving/disapproving return to service and that AC 43-9C lists required record content (inspection type/description, date, hours/cycles/life limits, signature/certificate number/kind of certificate, and the certifying statement) [S1][S4]. The excerpts do not provide the substantive approval criteria or procedures under Part 43.

Where to look:
- FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf | FAA Airworthiness Directive | location 6 – § 43.11 Content, form, and disposition of records for inspections conducted under parts 91 and 125 and §§ 135.411(a)(1) and 135.419; mentions the person approving or disapproving for return to service [S1].
- FAA_AC_43-9C_Maintenance_Records.pdf | FAA Airworthiness Directive | location 2 – Maintenance record requirements, responsibilities under Part 43 § 43.9, and required record content (inspection type/description, date, hours/cycles/life limits, signature/certificate number/kind of certificate, certifying statement) [S4].
- FAA_AC_00-56B_Distributor_Accreditation_Program.pdf | FAA Advisory Circular | location 13 – Requirements for imported parts and airworthiness approval documentation (not Part 43 return-to-service criteria) [S2].

query: How is a major repair or major alteration recorded and approved under FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B?
answer:
Direct answer:
Under FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix B, major repairs and major alterations for products not produced under an FAA approval must be recorded on the repair or alteration form specified in §§ 43.5(b) and 43.9(d); however, such recording is not required for products produced under an FAA approval [S1]. Major repairs and major alterations that have all necessary DER or ODA-approved technical data do not require further approval [S6]. The person intending to perform the work is responsible for obtaining the approved technical data [S2]. A major alteration report describes the work performed, the FAA-approved technical data used, and identifies the individual who performed and/or issued the approval for return to service; this is distinct from a major repair record [S7].

Where to look:
- FAA 14 CFR Part 43 Maintenance (regulation text on recording requirements and exceptions): FAA_14_CFR_Part_43_Maintenance.pdf, location 2 [S1]
- FAA AC 43-210A (data approval guidance for major repairs/alterations): FAA_AC_43-210A_Approval_Major_Repairs_Alterations_Data.pdf, location 5 [S2]
- FAA AC 43-210A (DER/ODA data sufficiency exception): FAA_AC_43-210A_Approval_Major_Repairs_Alterations_Data.pdf, location 10 [S6]
- FAA AC 43.13-2C (alteration data context; note it generally pertains to minor alterations but may be used for major): FAA_AC_43.13-2C_Aircraft_Alterations.pdf, location 14 [S4]

query: What electrical load analysis requirements apply when performing an aircraft alteration under FAA AC 43.13-2C?
answer:
Direct answer:
Under FAA AC 43.13-2C, the total system load (battery recharging plus system loads) must not exceed the pre-established electrical capacity of the generator system [S8]. Additionally, for repairs or alterations that do not change limitations, procedures, performance, or loading information, a supplement may consist of system operating instructions only, implying such cases may not require full load analysis documentation beyond operational instructions [S7].

- FAA AC 43.13-2C Aircraft Alterations, location 152: "Total system load (battery recharging plus system loads) must not exceed the pre-established electrical capacity of the generator system." [S8]
- FAA AC 43.13-2C Aircraft Alterations, location 19: "Repairs or alterations that do not result in a change to limitations, procedures, performance, or loading information may not require a supplement, or the supplemental information may consist of system operating instructions only." [S7]

query: What shielding and electrical separation standards govern engine ignition exciter circuits under AC 33.28-1?
answer:
Direct answer:
The supplied excerpts do not establish shielding and electrical separation standards specifically for engine ignition exciter circuits under AC 33.28-1. The only excerpt that addresses shielding, wire routing, and segregation is [S1], but it refers generally to "wire routing, shielding, and segregation outside the fuel tanks" in the context of evaluating short-circuit effects on FQIS components and wiring, not specifically to ignition exciter circuits or AC 33.28-1 requirements [S1]. Excerpt [S3] discusses EEC system architecture and separation of reverser control elements but does not cover ignition exciter shielding or electrical separation standards [S3]. Excerpt [S2] shows a capacitor-type ignition system schematic with an "exciter" component but provides no shielding or separation standards [S2].

Where to look:
- For general wire routing, shielding, and segregation outside fuel tanks (not specific to ignition exciter circuits): FAA Advisory Circular AC 25.981-1D, location 31 [S1].
- For ignition system schematics including an exciter in a capacitor-type system: FAA-H-8083-32B AMT Powerplant, Chapter 4, location 44 [S2].
- For EEC system separation and architecture (not ignition exciter shielding/separation): FAA Advisory Circular AC 33.28-1, location 19 [S3].

query: What is the effect of cathode-to-anode area ratio on localized galvanic corrosion rates in aircraft structure?
answer:
Direct answer:
The supplied excerpts do not establish the effect of cathode-to-anode area ratio on localized galvanic corrosion rates in aircraft structure. None of the provided passages quantify how changing that area ratio influences corrosion rate, nor do they present data linking area ratios to localized attack severity [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5].

What is missing
- No excerpt defines or measures "cathode-to-anode area ratio" in an aircraft structural context.
- No excerpt provides a relationship (qualitative or quantitative) between that ratio and the rate of localized galvanic corrosion.
- No excerpt discusses how area ratio affects current density distribution or pit initiation/growth on the anodic metal in aircraft structures.

Applicability note
- The excerpts cover general electrochemical corrosion mechanisms, specific alloy corrosion studies (magnesium, aluminum, Inconel/steel), and FAA guidance on electrolytic vs galvanic corrosion, but none address the area-ratio effect specifically [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5].

Where to look:
- For general galvanic corrosion mechanisms: FAA Advisory Circular AC 43-206 CHG1 Avionics Corrosion, Chapter 2 discussion of electrolytic and galvanic corrosion [S4].
- For electrochemical reaction fundamentals (anodic/cathodic processes) relevant to corrosion but not area-ratio effects: NASA Corrosion Prevention Gas Turbines report, section on electrochemical corrosion [S5].
- For specific alloy corrosion behavior (magnesium, aluminum) without area-ratio analysis: NASA Magnesium Alloy AZ31B Corrosion Protection report [S2]; NASA Relative Stress Corrosion Cracking Aluminum Alloys report [S3]; NASA Galvanic Corrosion Dissimilar Alloys Inconel/Steel/Aluminum report [S1].
